📅 10 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

📅 10 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning.
  • The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline.
  • It has been revealed that the standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a fresh, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

It has been revealed that the standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Sources indicate that dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

It has been revealed that offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

Sources indicate that A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:.

The GIF below reveals the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

Industry observers note that the table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

According to recent reports, the loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only highlights up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Sources indicate that distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

According to recent reports, the student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

It has been revealed that want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.20107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.

arXiv:2611.21626v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Developer-facing vulnerability analysis should link a function-level warning to a source location and a supported explanation. Cascaded systems can propagate weak evidence despite plausible components. We present X-LocVul, a measurement-first audit of a modular C/C++ detector-localizer-explainer pipeline combining UniXCoder, CodeT5, and Qwen2.5-Coder. We test whether evidence passed across stages is useful, merely source-resident, or misleading. Under duplication and temporal-leakage controls, UniXCoder has higher point estimates than CodeBERT, but true-CWE supervision is statistically indistinguishable from a shuffled-CWE control on PR-AUC, MCC, and vulnerable-class F1. Raw generated statements fail exact source matching in 90.83% of cases. Fuzzy projection reaches 83.79% Top-1 accuracy and exceeds semantic projection by 1.59 percentage points, although its advantage over raw ranking is not established. In a randomized, condition-label-masked two-rater evaluation of 50 paired cases, a predicted line improves evidence support, whereas a predicted CWE improves no endpoint. Oracle evidence improves evidence support (Holm-adjusted p=0.00453) and CWE consistency (p=3.49 x 10^-7), but not root-cause quality after correction (p=0.250); unsupported claims remain common. A chronological stress test retains ranking signal (ROC-AUC 0.782; PR-AUC 0.110), while the transferred threshold yields zero recall and F1. The contribution is not a state-of-the-art claim, but an auditable account of evidence construction, transfer, and consumption. It separates source residency from localization correctness, auxiliary labels from semantic supervision, and predicted evidence from useful evidence. Public E4 scores regenerate all 15 tests; missing manifests, final prompts, and profiler logs bound stronger reproducibility claims.

arXiv:2611.22206v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by rollout: heavy-tailed responses leave engines idle as each step waits for the longest response. Asynchronous training masks, but does not eliminate, idle time. We distinguish imbalance waste (uneven placement and decode contention) from straggler waste (waiting for the longest response). Tail length, not average load, often sets the step bound. We propose TAILROLL, an online scheduler integrated into an open-source RL framework. It combines stateless in-flight migration and sufficiency-gated termination. Migration moves decoding requests between engines at chunk boundaries and resumes them with one re-prefill under a freeness-based, cost-aware tail-balancing policy. Termination stops a response when its GRPO group has enough completed samples for advantage estimation, masking its partial output from the training loss. Across ten configurations, TAILROLL reduces rollout bubble ratio by 21% to 74% and cross-engine KV-cache imbalance by 44% to 79%. In end-to-end RL training, it cuts rollout time by 24% to 34%, full step time by 21% to 22% on long-CoT RL, and p95 request latency by 28% to 37%, while raising generation throughput by up to 33% with comparable or higher final reward.

We investigate whether deliberative reasoning changes this relationship. Because attack success and poison detection alone do not reveal whether detected poison continues to influence the final answer, we use two complementary measures: Cordon Rate, the probability that a model detects poison and nevertheless produces a poison-aligned answer, conditioned on a non-poison-aligned no-RAG response; and Leakage Rate, the probability that poisoned context influences the answer despite an explicit instruction to ignore retrieved documents. Across 200 SciFact questions, we compare reasoning-disabled and reasoning-enabled configurations of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Plus. In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an key post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21783v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one owners notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

According to recent reports, voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Industry observers note that supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:.

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:.

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new).

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most key latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

It has been revealed that at 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

Both run on hardware you control.

Industry observers note that because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

It has been revealed that low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

According to recent reports, local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

According to recent reports, together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

arXiv:2611.22439v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.

arXiv:2611.21678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at https://github.com/yasirmahmud/RTLReviewBench.

Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (246 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.21632v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed. We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

Sometimes you meet a founder who is so good that you want to back them no matter what they are working on. Just as rarely, you meet a firm whose vision is so singular, it feels both inevitable and differentiated at the same time. When I first sat down with Ben and Asher Spector to discuss Flapping Airplanes, I felt both of these to be true at once.

Ben is a founder of Prod, which has rapidly become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley. Asher, one year Benâs senior, is a former debate champion turned Stanford statistics Ph.D. The brothers have an eye for raw talent, and aged 25 and 26 respectively, they are building the âyoung personâs AGI lab.â Their co-founder Aidan Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at Neuralink for three years while in college at Georgia Tech. Ben and Asher believe that raw talent â the type of people who would previously have gone on to do Ph.D.s or join quant firms â are the key to unlocking the next phase of AI development. This stands in sharp contrast to the approach of focusing on âbrand nameâ AI talent at any price, which seems so in vogue right now.

There is something else that is countercultural about this lab too: they recognize that scale alone is not enough. Indeed, the lab is predicated on this notion. There is only one Internet, and weâve run out of it. Data is the bottleneck today to further AI scaling, not compute. Todayâs AI models are wildly inefficient, something that Dwarkesh Patel has recently hammered home in his interviews with Andrej Karpathy, Richard Sutton and others. Flapping Airplanes is dedicated to searching for a more data-efficient AI. The companyâs name is a nod to a more biological notion of machine intelligence.

One of the fundamental debates right now in AI is around scaling vs. research. The scaling paradigm argues for dedicating a huge amount of societyâs resources, as much as the economy can muster, toward scaling up todayâs LLMs, in the hopes that this will lead to AGI. The research paradigm argues that we are 2-3 research breakthroughs away from an âAGIâ intelligence, and as a result, we should dedicate resources to long-running research, especially projects that may take 5-10 years to come to fruition.

While the divide between these two schools of thought is far from absolute â research breakthroughs make compute investments more efficient, and GPUs are required for net newly introduced research â they each lead to different tradeoffs. A compute-first approach would prioritize cluster scale above all else, and would heavily favor short-term wins (on the order of 1-2 years) over long-term bets (on the order of 5-10 years). A research-first approach would spread bets temporally, and should be willing to make lots of bets that have a low absolute probability of working, but that collectively expand the search space for what is possible.

One concern I have had is that by starving Ph.D. programs of talent, and by reallocating a lot of this talent to scale-oriented work (as opposed to fundamental research), we could actually push out the AGI timeline. As I noted in a previous blog post, âcorporate politics tends to favor in vogue, consensus ideas over more radical, unpopular ones â the very kinds of ideas that can take years to prove worthwhile, and which scientific breakthroughs often depend on.â Flapping Airplanes is explicitly intended to provide a Ph.D.-like experience â true research independence, long-time horizons â while bridging the pay gap between academia and Major Tech.

One of the biggest learnings of the last decade in AI is the dramatic economic value of fundamental scientific progress. Since academia seems ill-suited to compete with Big Tech on this dimension right now, especially in AI, Flapping Airplanes is taking this into their own hands. And they are focused on precisely the problem that is likely to define the next wave of AI: building models inspired by the data efficiency of biology. With that as a north star, the manufacturer will make bets in a variety of directions to get there.

Recent findings suggest that there are two coherent motives right now in AI. One is the profit motive, and this should inspire all application builders, given the tremendous opportunity ahead. As I have noted on many occasions, AI is so underpenetrated relative to the capability set available, it is likely to create a golden age for builders for many years to come. There is a large profit pool available, and we are in the very earliest stages of generating it.

In a recent development, the second coherent motive in AI is AGI, predicated on the belief that now that weâve unlocked a machine intelligence, we should push toward upleveling that intelligence. Economically, progress in this direction is likely to be extremely valuable. The question is how to take on this objective in an efficient way, with a reasonable probability that resources invested will translate into long-term positive results. Flapping Airplanes is a pure play in that direction.

One of the most attractive aspects for me in partnering with Flapping Airplanes was the team. I have met nearly every candidate that has interviewed at Flapping Airplanes, and certainly every person the tech giant has hired. This is one of the best teams Iâve ever seen assembled at the beginning of such an ambitious journey.

There are two core beliefs that make Flapping Airplanes different for top talent:.

A belief that young people have always unlocked fundamental science in the past (Einstein was 26 during his âMiracle Yearâ).

A conviction that AI research is not a mystical domain for experts, but a domain learnable by anyone that is smart and ambitious.

In a recent development, with just these two premises, Flapping Airplanes is at odds with a prestige-obsessed culture in the Valley right now. It is exactly this obsession with substance and with raw individual talent that made Ben so successful at Prod, and it is this âflame spottingâ ability that gives me confidence in the courageous effort that is now Flapping Airplanes.

Industry News: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (230 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2608.12253v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real customers. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21674v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (286 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.21623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents can now proposal, write, test, review, and revise code at a volume no human organization can inspect line by line. Final code review therefore cannot remain the primary organizational control for owning code changes. The Software Engineering (SE) Factory moves control into the process that produces the code. The Factory protocols define how work moves, what evidence must exist before it can proceed, and who owns the result. A deterministic protocol engine, implemented in conventional code rather than prompts, enforces those protocols by controlling stage transitions, requiring evidence, and invoking gates and human escalation, where needed, before work can advance. The SE Factory preserves human authority over consequential decisions and makes accountable acceptance possible without requiring humans to supervise every agent action. The SE Factory is not a dark factory. Humans remain in control by defining the scope and granularity of delegation, the boundaries and escalation conditions, and the consequential decisions that require accountable human judgment. We draw on our experience building three distinct SE Factory implementations, all of which have undergone multiple iterations and two of which are publicly available as open-source systems, into ten principles for conceiving, building, and operating SE Factories at scale, grounded in the organizational and technical realities of our implementations. We do not claim that these principles are exhaustive or constitute the only viable foundation for an SE Factory. Rather, we offer them as a conceptual scaffold and shared vocabulary for reasoning about SE Factories, evaluating their designs, and guiding their evolution. Our goal is to catalyze a community-wide dialogue that moves software engineering beyond controls designed for human-scale code production toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

Breaking: When Neural Collapse Fails to Route: Routing Drift in Continual Learning

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (256 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.

Tech Report: Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories.
  • According to recent reports, give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge.
  • According to recent reports, two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

According to recent reports, give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

According to recent reports, two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

According to recent reports, A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

Both systems refuse to compress.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

According to recent reports, so on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that highlights up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

In a recent development, delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:.

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Industry observers note that where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:.

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

Sources indicate that we give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.).

Industry observers note that both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

Recent findings suggest that appWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The prepares are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22607v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph mining, critical for applications ranging from biological interaction discovery to recommender systems. While Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results, they are fundamentally limited by the inadvertent suppression of high-frequency signals, as the recursive aggregation that stabilizes structural learning inherently leads to over-smoothing, rendering node representations indistinguishable in deep layers. This limitation is particularly severe in heterophilous graphs, where structural proximity does not imply feature similarity. In this paper, we propose DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), a novel inductive framework designed to break the over-smoothing barrier via a "controlled instability" mechanism. Unlike conventional methods relying on static structural heuristics, DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline. First, a Chaotic Injection Module utilizes the Logistic Map to diversify the feature manifold, exploiting sensitivity to initial conditions to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes. Second, to mitigate the aleatoric uncertainty introduced by chaotic dynamics, a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism applies soft-thresholding to filter noise and retain only high-confidence signals. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DLS effectively balances feature discrimination with robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in heterophilous settings while maintaining competitive efficiency on standard homophilous graphs.

Conventional AIOps research has produced effective detectors, localizers, and diagnostic models, yet surveys typically organize them by task, telemetry modality, or learning technique. Such taxonomies describe what a method predicts, but not which decisions it may make or which evidence justifies that authority. We survey the transition from AIOps pipelines to agentic service operations through three coupled lenses: capability, operational authority, and evaluation evidence. We first relate SOA, microservices, Kubernetes, service meshes, and serverless platforms to the incident lifecycle. We then review conventional AIOps methods and audit 22 language-model-enabled systems according to their evaluated behavior rather than their intended autonomy. The audit indicates that most systems remain copilots or read-only investigators. Only two exercise write authority; both use constrained action envelopes, and neither carries controlled production-outcome evidence. Building on these findings, we synthesize a four-plane reference architecture, evidence grades, an evaluation ladder, and a controlled adoption path. Together, these artifacts clarify which claims current evaluations support and what evidence is still required for dependable agentic service operations.

arXiv:2611.22427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.14505v3 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. Harness-based methods gain little or nothing on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning indicates substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth.

Recent findings suggest that olmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Industry observers note that custom-computed embeddings are now available for customers of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Recent findings suggest that global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Recent findings suggest that computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:.

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

According to recent reports, studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Industry observers note that because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

Sources indicate that the examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Sources indicate that similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

Sources indicate that to test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

According to recent reports, from 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates rapidly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:.

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

In a recent development, sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

According to recent reports, flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Recent findings suggest that custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's crucial to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sources indicate that sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.
